# Establishing connections

In R the [`DBI`](https://dbi.r-dbi.org/) package is important package that provides a consistent interface for connecting to and interacting with databases. It serves as a foundational layer for working with databases in R. It's used by higher-level packages like `dplyr` and `dbplyr` to connect to databases and perform SQL operations.

```{r}
# To install on conda "conda install -c r r-dbi"
install.packages("DBI")
library(DBI)
```

To connect to a PostgreSQL database you will need the `RPostgres` package.

```{r}
# To install on conda "conda install -c conda-forge r-rpostgres"
install.packages("RPostgres")
library(RPostgres)
```

To finally connect to the database you can execute the following code (with your own configuration settings):

```{r}
# Connect to a PostgreSQL database
con <- dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres(), 
                 dbname = "db_1",
                 host = "localhost",
                 port = 5432,
                 user = "postgres",
                 password = "password0134!")

# Execute a SQL query
query <- "SELECT * FROM student"
result <- dbGetQuery(con, query)

# Disconnect from the database. It is important to disconnect
# once finished since there is a maximum of a maximum of open connections
# dbDisconnect(con)
```

## Selecting data

Of course, you can also run more complex raw SQL queries:

```{r}
result <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM course_codes WHERE course_desc LIKE 'A%'")

result
```

If you need to fetch results one at a time you might want to use [`dbFetch()`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/DBI/versions/0.5-1/topics/dbFetch)

```{r}
query <- dbSendQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM course_codes WHERE course_desc LIKE 'A%'")
result <- dbFetch(query, n = 1)
result
```

The `dbplyr` package allows you to write R code that gets translated into SQL queries, similarly to what SQLAlchemy does in Python. It is an extension of the `dplyr` package specifically designed to work with databases. On future weeks we are going to see many `dplyr` methods to manipulate data. Since there is no much difference between the syntax of `dbplyr`and `dplyr`, this won't be covered in depth now, but you can see some examples of queries employing `dbplyr` methods below:
tbl = table

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

# Create a remote data table using dbplyr
remote_table <- tbl(con, "student")
```

can add SELECT as below
```{r}
# Example queries using dbplyr

# Basic selection
query1 <- remote_table %>%
  select(first_name, surname)
query1
```

add a filter which would be our WHERE clause
```{r}
# Filtering
query2 <- remote_table %>%
  filter(dob > "1988-01-01")
query2
```

sUMMARISE - 

```{r}
# Grouping and aggregation
query3 <- remote_table %>%
  summarise(unique_categories = n_distinct(prog_code))
query3
```

AGGREGATION - INNER JOIN

```{r}
# Joining tables
another_remote_table <- tbl(con, "course_codes")
query4 <- remote_table %>%
  inner_join(another_remote_table, by = "course_id")
query4
```

# Show table names

In R there is no need to reflect tables. You can use for example `dbListTables` passing the connection object to list all tables in the dataset.

```{r}
# Build a vector of table names: tables
tables <- dbListTables(con)

# Display structure of tables
str(tables)
```

You can also import all tables using [lapply](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/apply-lapply-sapply-and-tapply-in-r/)

```{r}
# Import all tables
tables <- lapply(tables, dbReadTable, conn = con)

# Print out tables
tables
```

## Extract ERD

Unfortunately in R there is no easy way to extract the ERD of a generic database. You might need to look for SQL queries that can return the metadata information for the specific DBMS you are trying to connect to. If you have access to PostgreSQL, you can generate the ERD straight from the pgAdmin interface as well, as depicted below.

# Exercises

1.  Connect to the PostgreSQL database containing the Student and Course_codes tables. Retrieve all columns from the STUDENT table. Display the first few rows of the result.

```{r}

# Connect to a PostgreSQL database
con <- dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres(), 
                 dbname = "db_1",
                 host = "localhost",
                 port = 5432,
                 user = "postgres",
                 password = "password0134!")

# Execute a SQL query
# Build a vector of table names: tables
tables <- dbListTables(con)
# 
# # Display structure of tables
str(tables)
# 
# return all column names for the table listed
dbListFields(con, 'student')
dbListFields(con, 'dept')
dbListFields(con, 'emp')
dbListFields(con, 'course_codes')

# give yuo a snapshot of the first 5 rows
student_df <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM student LIMIT 5;")
head(student_df)


query <- "SELECT * FROM student"
result <- dbGetQuery(con, query)
result

# or
# put lal tables into a vector
tables <- c("course_codes", "dept", "emp", "student")

# loop through the vector 
# paste() - joins strings together - concatenates strings *with* a separator
# paste0()- joins strings together - concatenates strings *without* any separator
# ctd - returns a string or vector of strins yuo cna assign to a vraiable
# returns a string doesn't automatically print...
# cat = concatenate and print
# prints strings directly to the console wihtout quotes for extra formatting..
for(tbl in tables){
  cat("Table:", tbl, "\n")
  df <- dbGetQuery(con, paste0("SELECT * FROM ", tbl, " LIMIT 8;"))
  print(df)
  cat("\n-----------------------\n")
}
# This will print the first 5 rows of each table in a readable way.

# dbListTables, dbListFields, dbGetQuery? all come from DBI package

```

```{r}
head(s_count_df)
```

4.  Retrieve the student number, program code, course description, and date of birth for each student. You will need to join the two tables

```{r}
# prog_code and course_code are different names in the two different tables course _codes and student
# hence join on course_id
stud_data_df <- dbGetQuery(con, "
select 
  student.student_number, 
  student.prog_code, 
  student.dob, 
  course_codes.course_desc 
FROM student 
INNER JOIN course_codes on 
  student.course_id = course_codes.course_id")
head(stud_data_df )
```

5.  Using `dplyr`, call `tbl()` to create remote table objects for both STUDENT. Filter the STUDENT data to retrieve students born in a specific year. Hint: you will need to use the [filter](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/filter.html) method.

```{r}
library(dplyr)

# Create a remote data table using dbplyr
remote_table <- tbl(con, "student")

# query 1
query1 <- remote_table %>%
  select(first_name, surname)
query1


# Filtering born after date
query2 <- remote_table %>%
  filter(dob > "1988-01-01")
query2

# Filtering born in specific year
query2 <- remote_table %>%
  filter(sql(extract(year from dob) == 1989))
query2

# library(dplyr)

# Filter students born in 1989
query2 <- remote_table %>%
  filter(sql("EXTRACT(YEAR FROM dob) = 1989"))

# Execute query and collect results
query2_df <- query2 %>% collect()
query2_df



# the below all come from dbplyr and dplyr
# tbl()	dbplyr (built on top of dplyr)	Creates a remote table reference to a database table.
# select(), filter(), mutate(), summarise(), arrange(), %>%

# even though dplyr isn't explicitly called the functions are coming from it#
# functions like select() and filter() come from dplyr, 
# but dbplyr extends them so they work on remote database tables (like your PostgreSQL connection).
# tbl() → comes from dbplyr
# 
# filter(), select(), %>% → come from dplyr
# 
# Together, they let you write R code that runs SQL under the hood
# 
# ✅ Yes — your code is using dplyr (through dbplyr).

```

6.  Retrieve the average age of students in each program using the dob column and the current date.

```{r}

# the below works
query_avg_age_per_prog <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT 
      s.course_id,
      ROUND(AVG(EXTRACT(YEAR FROM AGE(CURRENT_DATE, s.dob))), 2) AS average_age
  FROM 
      student s
  GROUP BY 
      s.course_id
  ORDER BY 
      s.course_id;
")

query_avg_age_per_prog

# use join wityh couse_codes to get course code and description
#, 2 >> ROUND (number, decinal places) ,2 is the number of decimals
query_avg_age_per_prog <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT 
      c.course_code,
      c.course_desc,
      ROUND(AVG(EXTRACT(YEAR FROM AGE(CURRENT_DATE, s.dob))), 2) AS average_age
  FROM student AS s
  INNER JOIN course_codes AS c
      ON s.course_id = c.course_id
  GROUP BY c.course_code, c.course_desc
  ORDER BY c.course_code;
")
query_avg_age_per_prog


### 
# 2️⃣ Applying it to average age
# AVG(EXTRACT(YEAR FROM AGE(CURRENT_DATE, s.dob)))
# 
# 
# EXTRACT(YEAR FROM AGE(...)) → calculates the whole years for each student
# 
# AVG(...) → takes the average of those ages across all students in a group
# 
# Now, the result of AVG() might be something like 35.6666667.
# 
# ROUND(..., 2) → rounds this value to 2 decimal places, giving 35.67.
#
# 3️⃣ Example
# 
# Suppose we have three students with ages: 30, 32, 34
# 
# Average: (30 + 32 + 34) / 3 = 32
# 
# Rounded to 2 decimals: ROUND(32, 2) → still 32.00
# 
# Suppose ages were: 30, 33, 34
# 
# Average: (30 + 33 + 34)/3 = 32.3333
# 
# Rounded to 2 decimals: ROUND(32.3333, 2) → 32.33
# 
# ✅ The , 2 simply controls how precise your rounded average is.

```

7.  Challenge! Create a bar chart using [`ggplot2`](https://r-graph-gallery.com/218-basic-barplots-with-ggplot2.html) to visualize the distribution of student birth years. Hint: you might need to convert int64 types to numeric.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

# step 1 - get student data from database
student_yrob <- dbGetQuery(con, "
select
  student.first_name,
  student.surname,
  student.dob
from student
")

head(student_yrob)

# 2 extract the birth year
# mutate() method mofifies a variable - creat en ew avriables with functinos of existing variables (from book)
# dplyr functions  = filter(), arrange(), select (), mutate(), summarize() 
# can use with group_by which cnahnges the scope of each function from operating on whole dataset to operating on group by group
# structure of use >> fn(dataframe, arguments to describe what to do, result in a new df))

# format(dob, "%Y") extracts the year as a string
# as.numeric() converts it to numeric (important if you want proper ordering in the plot)
student_birth_yr <- student_yrob %>%
  mutate(birth_year = as.numeric(format(dob, "%Y"))) # birth_year is a new column mame


# 3 count students per birth year
student_year_counts <- student_birth_yr %>%
  # this is the dplyr version of GROUP BY In SQL, GROUP BY changes the scope of aggregation functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, etc.) so they are calculated per group instead of over the whole table.
  # In R with dplyr, group_by() works the same way: it sets the grouping context for subsequent operations like summarise() or mutate().
  group_by(birth_year) %>% # <-- use the column name, not the dataframe - groups the data by birth year
  summarise(count = n()) %>% # counts rows within each group
  ungroup() # removes the grouping, so any later operations act on the whole dhata frame again

# 4. plot the chart
# stat = "identity" → tells ggplot2 to use the count column directly.
# fill = "steelblue" → makes the bars look nicer.
# theme_minimal() → gives a clean background.

ggplot(student_year_counts, aes(x = birth_year, y = count)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Student Birth Years",
    x = "Birth Year",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

8.  Close the connection to the database.

```{r}
dbDisconnect(con)

```
